title: UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court
gist: Interview with UK Labour MP Jess Asato, who was deepfaked via Grok on X and is suing xAI under GDPR and privacy law, arguing the harm was avoidable by design, calling for consent rights over likeness and product-style regulation of AI.

insights.claim: Asato's case against xAI rests on existing data protection law (GDPR) for processing her face and likeness without consent, and on privacy law, arguing that a video preparing a sexual assault reaches a criminal threshold.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: A GDPR-based claim could set precedent for AI-company liability for generated content; monitor defense filings.
insights.quote: my case is brought under existing law, the GDPR
insights.locator: So, my case is brought under existing law

insights.claim: After repeated reports to X were dismissed as not violating its terms, a lawyer's letter got the images removed, and the lawyer then advised that xAI may have broken the law.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Platform self-moderation failed here; legal pressure worked where reporting did not.
insights.locator: Each of these things we reported to X

insights.claim: xAI's defense is expected soon but there is no timetable, and a hearing would follow only if there is a case to answer.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Litigation timing is uncertain; no near-term catalyst date.
insights.locator: So like with a lot of legal cases

insights.claim: xAI (now rebranded as SpaceXAI/SpaceXSI per the editors) was subpoenaed by New York City Council and did not attend initially, while four other frontier AI companies did, and it later had its hearing.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: xAI's reluctance to engage regulators is a governance and reputational signal.
insights.locator: You were in New York recently

insights.claim: Asato argues the Grok scandal was avoidable because other AI tools already refuse nudification prompts, so a general-purpose chatbot becoming a nudification tool reflected a design choice.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Safeguards are technically feasible; lax design raises legal and regulatory exposure for xAI.
insights.locator: So what was it particularly about the Grok scandal

insights.claim: The UK government accelerated a ban on nudification apps through the Crime and Policing Act and brought all AI chatbots under the Online Safety Act, but the law awaits a consultation before taking effect.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: UK chatbot regulation is legislated but not yet in force; watch consultation and commencement.
insights.locator: What I did was I talked about

insights.claim: The Online Safety Act originally excluded AI chatbots, and amendments to include them failed, which Asato says left the UK in a worse position.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Legislative gap shows how fast AI products outrun regulation.
insights.locator: The problem was, of course, that act

insights.claim: Asato says AI-generated child sexual abuse material is exploding, and that digital products should be regulated like other products because the harms are predictable and can be designed out.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Product-safety framing for AI points toward design-duty regulation.
insights.quote: we should be seeing digital product regulation in the same way as we would any other product regulation.
insights.locator: In the end it comes down to the people who create the products

insights.claim: Asato proposes a new legal and social norm that a person's picture, voice, and moving image are personal data not to be used by AI without consent, with exceptions for parody and satire of public figures.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Likeness rights could expand regulation beyond sexual deepfakes to political disinformation and generative media.
insights.locator: Could we create a greater right over our likeness online

insights.claim: Asato warns that a hyperrealistic video of a politician saying something they did not say, followed by real-world harm, is close.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Election-integrity risk from deepfakes may push legislation.
insights.quote: We are so close to a moment
insights.locator: Could we create a greater right over our likeness online

insights.claim: Asato says the central myth about deepfakes is that they come without harm, and that victims often cannot identify the creator or platform, leaving little recourse.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Harm severity and untraceability strengthen the case for platform liability.
insights.quote: That it comes without any harm.
insights.locator: I think you've already touched on it

insights.claim: The creator of the video targeting Asato was identified by police but lives in the US, so no charge could be brought, which she says makes cross-border enforcement akin to whack-a-mole without international agreement.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional gaps limit criminal enforcement; civil suits against companies are the practical route.
insights.locator: The person who made that horrible video

insights.claim: Asato says decisions on racing to superintelligence sit outside democratic structures and criticizes accepting cited extinction-risk estimates of 2, 10, or 20 percent that would be unacceptable in bridge or aircraft building; the government rejected a proposed kill switch bill.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: UK appetite for frontier-AI hard controls is limited for now, though political pressure persists.
insights.locator: So, yes, there have been proposals put forward for a kill switch

insights.claim: Asato says X's UK user base is skewed toward men, which she partly attributes to misogyny and abuse on the platform.
insights.speaker: Rosie Swash
insights.so_what: Platform safety can influence demographic composition and advertiser appeal.
insights.locator: I think it's really interesting when you look at X
